Survey on AI Ethics: A Socio-technical PerspectiveMbiazi Dave, Meghana Bhange, Maryam Babaei, Ivaxi Sheth, Patrik Kenfack, and Samira Ebrahimi KahouPublished in Computational Intelligence, 2025JournalThe past decade has observed a significant advancement in AI, with deep learning-based models being deployed in diverse scenarios, including safety-critical applications. As these AI systems become deeply embedded in our societal infrastructure, the repercussions of their decisions and actions have significant consequences, making the ethical implications of AI deployment highly relevant and essential. The ethical concerns associated with AI are multifaceted, including challenging issues of fairness, privacy and data protection, responsibility and accountability, safety and robustness, transparency and explainability, and environmental impact. These principles together form the foundations of ethical AI considerations that concern every stakeholder in the AI system lifecycle. In light of the present ethical and future x-risk concerns, governments have shown increasing interest in establishing guidelines for the ethical deployment of AI. This work unifies the current and future ethical concerns of deploying AI into society. While we acknowledge and appreciate the technical surveys for each of the ethical principles concerned, in this paper, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview that not only addresses each principle from a technical point of view but also discusses them from a social perspective.PaperPDFCiteCopy@article{mbiazi2025survey,

Fairness Under Demographic Scarce Regime
text:
Patrik KenfackPhD Candidate,Computer ScienceMontréal QC, CanadaÉTS Montréal & MilaGoogle ScholarLinkedInGitHubEmail


Fairness Under Demographic Scarce RegimePatrik Kenfack, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou, Ulrich AïvodjiPublished in Transactions on Machine Learning Research, 2024JournalMost existing works on fairness assume the model has full access to demographic information. However, there exist scenarios where demographic information is partially available because a record was not maintained throughout data collection or for privacy reasons. This setting is known as demographic scarce regime. Prior research has shown that training an attribute classifier to replace the missing sensitive attributes (proxy) can still improve fairness. However, using proxy-sensitive attributes worsens fairness-accuracy tradeoffs compared to true sensitive attributes. To address this limitation, we propose a framework to build attribute classifiers that achieve better fairness-accuracy tradeoffs. Our method introduces uncertainty awareness in the attribute classifier and enforces fairness on samples with demographic information inferred with the lowest uncertainty. We show empirically that enforcing fairness constraints on samples with uncertain sensitive attributes can negatively impact the fairness-accuracy tradeoff. Our experiments on five datasets showed that the proposed framework yields models with significantly better fairness-accuracy tradeoffs than classic attribute classifiers. Surprisingly, our framework can outperform models trained with fairness constraints on the true sensitive attributes in most benchmarks. We also show that these findings are consistent with other uncertainty measures such as conformal prediction.PaperPDFCodeVideoCiteCopy@article{

Patrik KenfackPhD Candidate,Computer ScienceMontréal QC, CanadaÉTS Montréal & MilaGoogle ScholarLinkedInGitHubEmail


On the Fairness of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)Patrik Kenfack, Daniil Arapov, Rasheed Hussain, S.M. Ahsan Kazmi, Adil KhanPublished in International Conference "Nonlinearity, Information and Robotics" (NIR), 2021ConferenceGenerative adversarial networks (GANs) are one of the greatest advances in AI in recent years. With their ability to directly learn the probability distribution of data and then sample synthetic realistic data. Many applications have emerged, using GANs to solve classical problems in machine learning, such as data augmentation, class imbalance problems, and fair representation learning. In this paper, we analyze and highlight the fairness concerns of GANs. In this regard, we show empirically that GANs models may inherently prefer certain groups during the training process and therefore they’re not able to homogeneously generate data from different groups during the testing phase. Furthermore, we propose solutions to solve this issue by conditioning the GAN model towards samples’ groups or using the ensemble method (boosting) to allow the GAN model to leverage distributed structure of data during the training phase and generate groups at an equal rate during the testing phase.PaperPDFCiteCopy@inproceedings{kenfack2021fairness,

title: The “Hidden” Ensemble Inside Tabular Foundation Models
text:
A tabular foundation model (TFM) is a transformer-based model that predicts your test labels in one forward pass using your training data as context. The model is frozen, so it does not update its weights on your data. It is a foundation model because it is pre-trained on thousands (or millions) of tables, and it is tabular because it takes a table as input. TFMs are the new hotness in tabular machine learning, and they are starting to appear in production.
The definition above is consistent with what you would generally find in the literature. It states that TFMs make one forward pass. In practice, they don’t. The default configurations of TFMs such as TabICLv2, TabFM, TabPFNv3 and Mitra each run the model several times on perturbed copies of your training data and average the answers. The perturbations are things like shuffling the columns, shuffling the class labels, or changing the preprocessing (e.g., using different feature normalization techniques).
Each snippet is the whole API: fit, then predict. Nothing in it mentions an ensemble. But with the default settings, a single predict call runs the network once per ensemble member (8 for TabICLv2, 32 for TabFM). Each member sees a different version of your table: the columns in a different order, the class labels shifted, and one of the preprocessing options (no normalization or a power transform). The final prediction is the average over members. What looks like one forward pass is really 8 or 32, and the second block in each snippet spells out the settings that were applied silently. The default budgets differ (8 members for TabICLv2, 32 for TabFM); in the experiments below I evaluate up to 32 members for both.
This ensemble ships as a default and is rarely ablated. I wanted to know what it actually does, so I opened up the two strong open models I could instrument, TabICLv2 and TabFM, and ran them on all 51 TabArena datasets (30 binary, 8 multiclass, 13 regression).

objectID: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#what-i-did
href: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#what-i-did
title: The “Hidden” Ensemble Inside Tabular Foundation Models
text:
What I did
I modified the inference loop of each model so that every ensemble member’s prediction is cached. After that, the number of members, which perturbations are included and how members are averaged are all cheap post-hoc operations. About 48,000 cached cells later, I could ask questions that would otherwise cost a GPU run each.
I use two scales throughout:

Elo rating, computed the way TabArena does it (pairwise wins across datasets and splits). Mine is local: it comes from a pool of my own configurations, not the official leaderboard pool.
Effect size in the task’s own metric: AUC for binary, log-likelihood for multiclass, relative RMSE reduction for regression, with a paired Wilcoxon test over datasets.

objectID: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#the-ensemble-earns-a-lot-of-elo-for-very-little-accuracy
href: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#the-ensemble-earns-a-lot-of-elo-for-very-little-accuracy
title: The “Hidden” Ensemble Inside Tabular Foundation Models
section: 1. The ensemble earns a lot of Elo for very little accuracy
text:
1. The ensemble earns a lot of Elo for very little accuracy
Against a single forward pass, the shipped ensembles earn between 168 and 230 Elo. In the task’s own metric, that is (Table 1):



Table 1: Effect of the shipped ensemble versus a single forward pass.









Task
Gain from the shipped ensemble




Binary
about 0.001 AUC (0.0012 for TabICLv2, 0.0014 for TabFM)


Multiclass
0.002 to 0.003 log-likelihood


Regression
0.7% to 0.9% lower RMSE






The gain is real and consistent. TabFM’s ensemble beats a single pass on 27 of 30 binary datasets, and on all 13 regression datasets. But a thousandth of AUC is a thousandth of AUC.






Figure 1: Local Elo gain against effect size, for every configuration of both models I ran. Colour is the model. Circles are the native perturbation views (column shuffling, class shuffling, preprocessing, and their combinations), squares are column subsampling (each member sees only some of the columns), and triangles are row subsampling (each member sees only some of the rows). The horizontal axes are symmetric-log.



Figure 1 puts every configuration on both scales. They all fall on one monotone curve, and it is steep. A method that wins by a small margin on most datasets earns a large Elo. Elo tells you the ensemble helps consistently. It does not tell you how much. I would read it as a statement about consistency and report an effect size next to it.






Important



My Elo pool contains many near-copies of each other, which probably amplifies the effect. I haven’t computed Elo against the official TabArena pool yet, and I expect the curve to be flatter there.

objectID: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#the-32-members-are-almost-one-member
href: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#the-32-members-are-almost-one-member
title: The “Hidden” Ensemble Inside Tabular Foundation Models
section: 2. The 32 members are almost one member
text:
2. The 32 members are almost one member
The shipped ensembles average 32 members (fewer for TabICLv2 on some tasks). I measured how many independent predictions that is, using the participation ratio of the members’ error correlation. The median pool carries between 1.0 and 1.2 effective members.
So the members are close to copies of each other. Perturbing the input of a frozen network barely changes what it believes. That fits the size of the gains above.
Most of the gain also arrives early. A single perturbed member is actually worse than the unperturbed pass, so the ensemble first has to recover its own damage. After that, returns diminish quickly (Figure 2).1






Figure 2: Gain over a single pass against the number of forward passes, for each model’s shipped recipe. Shaded bands are 95% bootstrap CIs over datasets. TabICLv2’s curves stop where its recipe runs out of distinct members.



Take TabFM on binary tasks. One member scores about 0.0002 AUC below the single pass. Four members give +0.0011, eight give +0.0013, and 32 give +0.0014. Going from 8 to 32 members quadruples the cost and adds about 0.00016 AUC. On regression the pattern is the same: 0.60% lower RMSE at 8 members and 0.68% at 32. In Elo terms, 8 members reach 78% to 84% of the 32-member gain for TabFM, and 16 members reach 89% to 94% (Figure 3).






Figure 3: Local Elo gain over a single pass as the number of members grows. Each line is a different perturbation view: column shuffling, class shuffling, preprocessing, or a combination of them; “default (shipped) mix” is the model’s own default recipe. Top row: TabICLv2. Bottom row: TabFM. Shaded bands are 95% bootstrap CIs.

objectID: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#column-shuffling-class-shuffling-and-preprocessing-explain-the-gain
href: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#column-shuffling-class-shuffling-and-preprocessing-explain-the-gain
title: The “Hidden” Ensemble Inside Tabular Foundation Models
section: 3. Column shuffling, class shuffling and preprocessing explain the gain
text:
3. Column shuffling, class shuffling and preprocessing explain the gain
The shipped recipes mix three perturbations: column shuffling, class shuffling and preprocessing. I decomposed the gain over them with Shapley values, and I also tried the full product of all three instead of the shipped mix.
On binary and regression tasks, the full product is no better than the shipped mix. The only possible exception is multiclass TabICLv2 (+0.003 log-likelihood, improving 7 of 8 datasets), but with 8 datasets the test gives p = 0.078, so I don’t count it as established. Which axis matters most depends on the model and the task: preprocessing carries about half the multiclass gain for TabICLv2, while class shuffling matters most for TabFM. I wouldn’t expect that ordering to transfer.

objectID: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#giving-each-member-less-of-the-table-never-helps
href: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#giving-each-member-less-of-the-table-never-helps
title: The “Hidden” Ensemble Inside Tabular Foundation Models
section: 4. Giving each member less of the table never helps
text:
4. Giving each member less of the table never helps
Classical ensemble methods such as bagging and random forests give each member only part of the table: a random subset of rows, or a random subset of columns. The hope is that each member will learn something different, and averaging will reduce variance. I tested these tricks on top of the shipped recipe (Table 2).



Table 2: Change versus the shipped recipe when each member sees only part of the table. Every row is a loss or no change.











Each member keeps…
TabICLv2
TabFM
p




Half of the columns (binary)
−0.0045 AUC
−0.0048 AUC
< 0.001


Half of the rows (binary)
−0.0025 AUC
−0.0022 AUC
< 0.001


90% (classification)
neutral
neutral
—


90% of the rows (regression)
0.4% higher RMSE
0.3% higher RMSE
< 0.01






I did not find a setting where withholding information beats the shipped recipe. This suggests that the ensemble’s gain comes from averaging over perturbations, not from decorrelating independent fits. The members are too similar to each other for subsampling to help. The model is frozen, so no member learns anything substantially different from the others. The ensemble is a variance-reduction step, not a way to add new information.

But what about round-robin subsampling?
Some wrappers deal columns out round-robin, with the argument that every column is then seen by some member. That sounds like it should fix the information loss, so I tested it directly against random draws at the same budget (TabICLv2, 16 members, half the columns each).
It doesn’t. Round-robin gains +0.0007 AUC over random draws (p = 0.16), which is within noise, and it stays 0.0028 AUC below a single full-table pass. The reason is that coverage was never the problem: random draws already show almost every column to some member.2 What hurts is what each member cannot see, not which columns the ensemble misses.
Coverage only starts to matter when members keep almost everything. On binary tasks, leave-one-fold-out partitions that drop 12.5% of the columns per member match the shipped ensemble within noise. I only ran these designs for TabICLv2 at half the columns, so treat the round-robin result as specific to that setting.

objectID: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#two-additions-that-behave-differently
href: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#two-additions-that-behave-differently
title: The “Hidden” Ensemble Inside Tabular Foundation Models
text:
5. Two additions that behave differently

Relabelling categorical codes per member is a good example of the Elo gap. For TabICLv2 it earns +92 Elo on binary tasks, and the effect size is 0.0004 AUC with p = 0.15. A decent rating, and nothing measurable behind it.
Appending extra features (SVD projections, crosses) to TabFM does help on multiclass and regression tasks: +0.0010 log-likelihood on all 8 multiclass datasets (p = 0.008) and a 0.5% RMSE reduction on regression (p = 0.021). On binary tasks it does nothing. I don’t know why binary differs.

Aggregation also matters. TabFM’s extended configuration adds feature expansion, probability pooling and calibration. On multiclass tasks, most of its gain comes from the pooling and calibration, not from the members.

objectID: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#what-this-means-for-ensembling-tfms
href: blog/posts/The hidden ensemble in tabular foundation models/index.html#what-this-means-for-ensembling-tfms
title: The “Hidden” Ensemble Inside Tabular Foundation Models
section: What this means for ensembling TFMs
text:
What this means for ensembling TFMs
For classical models, ensembling is one of the most reliable ways to buy accuracy. Bagging and random forests average trees fit on different resamples of the data, and deep ensembles average networks trained from different initialisations. Each member is a genuinely different fit, so their errors are only partly correlated, and averaging removes a lot of variance. Those are well-established results, and I did not rerun them here.
A TFM ensemble is a different animal. Every member is the same frozen network, reading the same table in a slightly different presentation. Nothing is refit, so there is no independent fit to average. The results above are what you would expect from that: members that are close to copies of each other (about one effective member out of 32), and a gain of roughly \(10^{-3}\) AUC. The ensemble works as a small variance-reduction step. It does not add new information.
I think this calls for rethinking ensembling for TFMs, rather than copying the recipes from trees and neural networks:

Don’t import the classical recipe as is. Shuffling and re-preprocessing the input is cheap, but it is not where the diversity of a tree or deep ensemble comes from, and it shouldn’t be expected to give similar gains.
Treat withholding information as a poor source of diversity. Subsampling columns or rows is the standard way to decorrelate bagged models. For a frozen TFM, the information each member loses costs more than the diversity it adds.
Look at the other levers. Adding features helped in some tasks, and pooling and calibration mattered more than the members in others. Sources of diversity that go beyond one frozen network, such as different checkpoints or different models, are the obvious next thing to test. I haven’t tested them here.
Report an effect size next to Elo. Elo says whether an ensemble wins consistently. It doesn’t say by how much, and for TFMs the gap between those two is large.
Automate the choice of perturbations. The best mix of preprocessing steps and perturbation axes depends on the dataset. TabFM-auto uses a language-model agent (such as Gemini) to evolve the processing pipeline for each dataset, which works especially well when column names hint at feature types. It costs more (several forward passes plus agent loops), but it is a promising direction for automating TFM pipelines.

title: Getting Started with Compute Clusters
text:
Digital Research Alliance of Canada
Digital Research Alliance of Canada is a national research infrastructure that provides high-performance computing resources to researchers across Canada. It is a partnership between the Canadian government and the private sector.
If you don’t have an account, you can sign up here. You will need to get sponsored by your supervisor to get your account approved.

title: Getting Started with Compute Clusters
text:
Login to Compute Canada
Once you have an account, you can login via ssh to the cluster. In case you don’t have ssh installed on your computer, you should follow the instructions here to install it.
Compute Canada has several compute clusters located across Canada. Here is short list of those clusters:

Graham
Cedar
Narval
Beluga







TipCluster Names



The names of the clusters are chosen based some facts about the location of the cluster. For example, Beluga, located at École de technologie supérieure in Montreal, is named after the Beluga whale, which is found in the St. Lawrence River.


The name of the cluster is used to login to a specific cluster. For example, to login to the Beluga cluster, you can use the following command:
ssh <your_username>@beluga.alliancecan.ca

title: Getting Started with Compute Clusters
text:
Login nodes vs Compute nodes
Unlike other cloud providers, login via ssh to a node does not give direct access to a compute machine. Instead, you will be on a login node from which you can submit jobs to the compute nodes.

Login nodes
Once you are logged in to the cluster, you will be on a login node. Login nodes are meant for interactive use and are not meant for running your large programs.
Things you can do on the login nodes:

Git clone your repository
Run small interactive jobs (will be discussed below)
Edit and submit jobs using a text editor
View the status of your jobs
Transfer files to and from the cluster
Create virtual environments and install packages
Submit jobs to the cluster (will be assigned to a compute node)

Things you cannot do on the login nodes:

Run large jobs
Use a lot of memory
Use a lot of CPU




Example of ssh session on a login node. Login nodes generally have hostnames like beluga1, beluga2, etc.




Compute nodes
Compute nodes are meant for running large jobs. They have more memory and CPU than login nodes, and they have GPUs.
When you submit a job, it is assigned to a compute node with the requested resources. We will get back to this below. Before that, let’s discuss file systems and where you should copy the files for your project.

title: Getting Started with Compute Clusters
text:
File System
One of the most important thing to know about Compute Canada is the file system. There are three types of file systems with different properties and limitations: home, project, scratch
 Directory structure on Beluga
The home directory has small quota, a fixed number of filesystem objects and smaller storage space (generally up to 25 GB) and has dearly backups. The project directory is meant for long-term storage of data that is shared across users linked to a sponsor. The scratch directory is meant for temporary storage of data and has a larger fixed quota per user and a larger storage space (generally above to 2 PB of space).






Tip



If you are actively working on a project, I recommend that you copy your data (source code, datasets, etc.) to the scratch directory. This will save you time, and you don’t need to worry about the storage space. You can copy your data back to the project directory after your project is done or paused.


Note that only the unused files on the scratch directory are deleted after 30 or 60 days, depending on the cluster. So if you are actively working on your project, you can use scratch and run everything as on your local machine, with logs files and results saved in your project directory.
A better approach is to have your source code and data in the project directory and make sure your logs (e.g., training logs and models’ checkpoints) and results are saved in the scratch directory. This way you can keep your project directory clean and you can have better control of your data. In another post, we will discuss how to speed up jobs using $SLURM_TMPDIR.

title: Getting Started with Compute Clusters
text:
Job Submission
Once you have your data in the scratch directory, you can submit a job to the cluster.

Module loading
Before running any job, you need to load the modules for the software you need. For example, if you need to use Python 3.10, you need to load the Python module with the following command.
module load python/3.10
After loading the module, you can check if it is loaded correctly by running module list. Note that from here on, all the dependencies you install, with pip install for example, will be installed for this specific version of Python and will be available in your environment every time you load the module.


Virtual environment
After loading the module, you can also create a virtual environment for project-specific dependencies.
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate


Submitting a job
At this point, you should have your data in the scratch directory, installed the dependencies in your loaded module and created a virtual environment for project-specific dependencies.
Now you can submit a job to the cluster.
Let’s assume you have a Python script (my_script.py) that you want to run on the cluster, and you can pass some arguments to it, for example, the number of epochs and the dataset to use, etc. Normally, on your local machine, you run this script as follows:
python my_script.py --num_epochs 60 --dataset mnist
To submit this job to the cluster, you need to create a job script that will be used to submit the job. A job script is a bash program that will load the necessary modules and specify the resources your Python program needs (number of nodes, number of cores, amount of memory, type and number of GPUs, etc.).

Job script directives
The header of the job script contains directives to specify the resources your Python program needs. Here is an example of a job script header:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=YOUR-PI-ACCOUNT
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node=1         # Number of GPU(s) per node
#SBATCH --node=1         # Number of GPU(s) per node
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4         # CPU cores/threads
#SBATCH --time=00:15:00           # Time limit in hh:mm:ss 
#SBATCH --mem=1024M

#SBATCH --account=YOUR-PI-ACCOUNT is the account of your PI, often def-username. To obtain what account you have access to, you can login to CCDB and click on My Account -> My Resources and Allocations




The illustration above tells you what account you can use on a given cluster. For example, on Cedar, I can submit jobs using #SBATCH --account=YOUR-PI-ACCOUNT.



#SBATCH --gpus-per-node=1 is the number of GPUs per node, in general, you set up 4 GPUs per node. And #SBATCH --node=1 specifies the number of nodes you want to use.
If you want to use 2 GPUs per node, you can set #SBATCH --gpus-per-node=2 and #SBATCH --node=1
If you want to use 2 nodes with 4 GPUs per node, you can set #SBATCH --gpus-per-node=4 and #SBATCH --node=2, i.e., your job will be using 8 GPUs in total.
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4 is the number of CPU cores per task. This is the number of CPU cores your program will use.
#SBATCH --time=00:15:00 is the time limit for your job. This is the maximum time your job can run. In general, you don’t know exactly how long your job will run, so you should set a time limit that is long enough to run your job and adjust it later.
#SBATCH --mem=1024M is the amount of memory your job will use. This is the maximum amount of memory your job can use. You can set it in GB as --mem=32G you request 32 GB of memory. If you are not sure how much memory your job will use, you can set it to a large value and adjust it later.

title: Getting Started with Compute Clusters
text:
Putting it all together
Here is an example of a job script that you can use to submit your job:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=YOUR-PI-ACCOUNT
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node=1         # Number of GPU(s) per node
#SBATCH --node=1         # Number of GPU(s) per node
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4         # CPU cores/threads
#SBATCH --time=00:15:00           # Time limit in hh:mm:ss 
#SBATCH --mem=1024M


module load python/3.10 # Load the Python module version
source .venv/bin/activate # Activate the virtual environment


python my_script.py --num_epochs 60 --dataset mnist
Finally, you can submit your job by running the following command:
sbatch my_script.sh # You will see a job ID in the output.
Depending on the cluster and the resources you requested, your job will be assigned to a compute node and will start running. A log file, named slurm-<job_id>.out, will be created in the main directory of your project.
You can check the status of your jobs by running the following command:
squeue -u <your_username>
In case you want to cancel your job, you can run the following command:
scancel <job_id>
If you want to cancel all your jobs, you can run the following command:
scancel -u <your_username>

title: Getting Started with Compute Clusters
text:
Interactive jobs
Sometimes you want to run a job interactively, for example, to debug your code or to run a small test. You can do this by running the following command:
salloc --time=00:30:00 --account=YOUR-PI-ACCOUNT --mem=48000 --gpus-per-node=4 --cpus-per-task=1
Similarly to job scripts, parameters of the salloc command specify the resources you need for your interactive job session.
The illustration below shows an interactive job session on the Beluga cluster.
 Interactive job session on the Beluga cluster
You can see that salloc moved us from a login node (beluga3) to a compute node (bg12103). This compute node has requested resources, i.e., 4 GPUs, 1 CPU core, 48 GB of memory and 30 minutes of time. However, before running your Python program interactively, you need to type commands to load the module and activate the virtual environment.






TipInteractive jobs



The more you request resources (time, GPUs, CPU cores, memory), the longer you will wait to get an interactive compute node. You can use them to test your code before submitting a job script.


In the next post, we will discuss how to speed up jobs using $SLURM_TMPDIR.

title: Getting Started with Compute Clusters
text:
Conclusion
In this post, we have covered the basics of compute clusters, including how to log in to the cluster, how to submit jobs, and how to use interactive jobs. I believe that from here on, you can navigate the documentation of the compute cluster to learn more options and best practices when using the cluster.
For more training material, you can check these beginner’s guides covering Linux commands, git & version control, and Python programming.

title: Impact of Model Ensemble On the Fairness of Classifiers in Machine Learning
text:
Patrik KenfackPhD Candidate,Computer ScienceMontréal QC, CanadaÉTS Montréal & MilaGoogle ScholarLinkedInGitHubEmail


Impact of Model Ensemble On the Fairness of Classifiers in Machine LearningPatrik Kenfack, Adil Khan; S.M. Ahsan Kazmi, Rasheed Hussain, Alma Oracevic, Asad Masood KhattakPublished in International Conference on Applied Artificial Intelligence (ICAPAI), 2021ConferenceMachine Learning (ML) models are trained using historical data that may contain stereotypes of the society (biases). These biases will be inherently learned by the ML models which might eventually result in discrimination against certain subjects, for instance, people with certain protected characteristics (race, gender, age, religion, etc.). Since the decision provided by ML models might affect people's lives, fairness of these models becomes crucially important. When training a model with fairness constraints, a significant loss in accuracy relative to the unconstrained model may be unavoidable. Reducing the trade-off between fairness and accuracy is an active research question within the fair ML community, i.e., to provide models with high accuracy with as little bias as possible. In this paper, we extensively investigate the fairness metrics over different ML models and study the impact of ensemble models on fairness. To this end, we compare different ensemble strategies and empirically show which strategy is preferable for different fairness metrics. Furthermore, we also propose a novel weighting technique that allows a balance between fairness and accuracy. In essence, we assign weights such that they are proportional to classifiers' performance in term of fairness and accuracy. Our experimental results show that our weighting technique reduces the trade-off between fairness and accuracy in ensemble models.PaperPDFCiteCopy@inproceedings{kenfack2021impact,

title: A Survey on Fairness Without Demographics
text:
Patrik KenfackPhD Candidate,Computer ScienceMontréal QC, CanadaÉTS Montréal & MilaGoogle ScholarLinkedInGitHubEmail


A Survey on Fairness Without DemographicsPatrik Kenfack, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou, Ulrich AïvodjiPublished in Transactions on Machine Learning Research, 2024JournalThe issue of bias in Machine Learning (ML) models is a significant challenge for the machine learning community. Real-world biases can be embedded in the data used to train models, and prior studies have shown that ML models can learn and even amplify these biases. This can result in unfair treatment of individuals based on their inherent characteristics or sensitive attributes such as gender, race, or age. Ensuring fairness is crucial with the increasing use of ML models in high-stakes scenarios and has gained significant attention from researchers in recent years. However, the challenge of ensuring fairness becomes much greater when the assumption of full access to sensitive attributes does not hold. The settings where the hypothesis does not hold include cases where (1) only limited or noisy demographic information is available or (2) demographic information is entirely unobserved due to privacy restrictions. This survey reviews recent research efforts to enforce fairness when sensitive attributes are missing. We propose a taxonomy of existing works and, more importantly, highlight current challenges and future research directions to stimulate research in ML fairness in the setting of missing sensitive attributes.PaperPDFCiteCopy@article{

title: Learning Fair Representations through Uniformly Distributed Sensitive Attributes
Adaptive Group Robust Ensemble Knowledge Distillation
text:
Patrik KenfackPhD Candidate,Computer ScienceMontréal QC, CanadaÉTS Montréal & MilaGoogle ScholarLinkedInGitHubEmail


Adaptive Group Robust Ensemble Knowledge DistillationPatrik Kenfack, Ulrich Aïvodji, Samira Ebrahimi KahouPublished in Transactions on Machine Learning Research | NeurIPS Algorithmic Fairness through the lens of Metrics and Evaluation Workshop, 2025JournalWorkshopNeural networks can learn spurious correlations in the data, often leading to performance degradation for underrepresented subgroups. Studies have demonstrated that the disparity is amplified when knowledge is distilled from a complex teacher model to a relatively ``simple'' student model. Prior work has shown that ensemble deep learning methods can improve the performance of the worst-case subgroups; however, it is unclear if this advantage carries over when distilling knowledge from an ensemble of teachers, especially when the teacher models are debiased. This study demonstrates that traditional ensemble knowledge distillation can significantly drop the performance of the worst-case subgroups in the distilled student model even when the teacher models are debiased. To overcome this, we propose Adaptive Group Robust Ensemble Knowledge Distillation (AGRE-KD), a simple ensembling strategy to ensure that the student model receives knowledge beneficial for unknown underrepresented subgroups. Leveraging an additional biased model, our method selectively chooses teachers whose knowledge would better improve the worst-performing subgroups by upweighting the teachers with gradient directions deviating from the biased model. Our experiments on several datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed ensemble distillation technique and show that it can even outperform classic model ensembles based on majority voting.PaperPDFCodePosterVideoCiteCopy@article{

title: Training Fair Tabular Foundation Models
Towards Fair In-Context Learning with Tabular Foundation Models
text:
Patrik KenfackPhD Candidate,Computer ScienceMontréal QC, CanadaÉTS Montréal & MilaGoogle ScholarLinkedInGitHubEmail


Towards Fair In-Context Learning with Tabular Foundation ModelsPatrik Kenfack, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou, Ulrich AïvodjiPublished in Transactions on Machine Learning Research | 1st ICML Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data (2025), 2026JournalWorkshopTransformer-based tabular foundation models have recently demonstrated promising in-context learning (ICL) performance on structured data, emerging as competitive alternatives to gradient-boosted trees. However, the fairness implications of this new paradigm remain largely unexplored. We present the first investigation of fairness in tabular ICL, evaluating three recently proposed foundation models--TabPFNv2, TabICL, and TabDPT--on multiple benchmark datasets. To mitigate biases, we explore three pre-processing fairness-enhancing methods: correlation removal (decorrelating input features from the sensitive attribute), group-balanced sample selection (ensuring equal representation of protected groups in context examples), and uncertainty-based sample selection (prioritizing context examples with high sensitive-attribute prediction uncertainty). Our experiments show that the uncertainty-based strategy consistently improves group fairness metrics (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity) with minimal impact on predictive accuracy.PaperPDFCodePosterVideoCiteCopy@article{
